_: The Numeris reference board. Each entry is one screen Thomas rates in tools/picker. `why` is the reason it is here, one line. Captured by scripts/src/reference-board-capture.ts; `copy` entries are taken from the vault instead of the web.
groups: personal data with a point of view

screens.title: Finviz S&P 500 map
screens.why: The whole market as one treemap: area is size, colour is the day, no chrome. The densest useful single screen in finance, and a replacement for the Bloomberg Terminal page, which refuses headless browsers.

screens.title: TradingView chart
screens.why: The chart is the whole page and the chrome collapses to thin rails; the one finance UI most people have actually chosen to look at for hours.

screens.title: Kraken Pro
screens.why: Order book, depth and ladder as a single dense instrument; it commits to being a workbench rather than a brochure.

screens.title: Binance spot
screens.why: The maximal case: six live panes, red and green only where they mean direction, everything else grey. Included to find where density stops being useful.

screens.title: Hyperliquid
screens.why: A newer terminal that kept the density and dropped the clutter: monospace figures, hairline grid, one accent.

screens.title: Koyfin
screens.why: Bloomberg's information layout rebuilt for a browser; dashboards of small multiples, tables that are actually tables.

screens.title: OpenBB
screens.why: The open-source terminal: a command line that draws charts, which is closer to Claude Code than to a fintech app.

screens.title: Interactive Brokers TWS
screens.why: Ugly on purpose and trusted for it: no rounded corners, no marketing, a grid of numbers professionals refuse to give up.

screens.title: FT markets data tearsheet
screens.why: A newspaper's data desk doing a terminal: serif headings over tabular numerals, salmon ground, no card in sight.

screens.title: Robinhood Legend
screens.why: A consumer brand building a desktop terminal; shows what the generic fintech look becomes when it tries to be serious.

screens.title: Ghostfolio (open-source wealth tracker, live demo)
screens.why: The closest open-source cousin to Numeris: a real portfolio app, dark, chart-led, and a useful test of whether that already reads as template.

screens.title: Linear
screens.why: The benchmark for product UI that is dense, keyboard-first and still calm; the standard 'Linear-grade' refers to.

screens.title: FRED (St. Louis Fed) series page
screens.why: Institutional and plain: one blue line, grey recession bands, the source and the units printed under the chart. Trust without styling.

screens.title: Our World in Data grapher
screens.why: A chart component with an opinion: labels on the lines instead of a legend, the table one tab away, download always visible.

screens.title: FT visual and data journalism
screens.why: The FT chart doctrine at scale: pink ground, one highlight colour, annotations written as sentences on the chart itself.

screens.title: The Pudding
screens.why: Data stories that scroll like essays; every chart is bespoke to its argument and none of them could be a dashboard widget.

screens.title: Reuters Graphics
screens.why: Wire-service restraint: black, white, one colour, large type, and maps and charts that carry the whole story.

screens.title: Sherwood (formerly Chartr)
screens.why: Chartr's newsletter charts grown into a newsroom: one colour per story and a headline written on the chart itself. Stands in for The Economist's Graphic detail, which returns 403 headless.

screens.title: D3 gallery on Observable
screens.why: Two hundred chart forms in one grid; the reminder that a figure can be a shape other than a bar, a ring or a line.

screens.title: FlowingData
screens.why: Personal data drawn by one person with a point of view; the charts are about a life, which is what a net worth chart is.

screens.title: Datawrapper blog
screens.why: The working notes of a chart tool that refuses decoration: every post is a rule about colour, labels or annotation with a before and after.

screens.title: GMUNK, Tron: Legacy boardroom
screens.why: The interfaces Thomas rated love on the Atrium run: dense, layered, luminous, every element on an axis, nothing hidden behind a hover.

screens.title: GMUNK, Oblivion GFX
screens.why: The lighter sibling: white ground, thin rules, radar and telemetry as a calm instrument rather than a glowing one.

screens.title: HUDS+GUIS, the screen-interface archive
screens.why: The archive of fictional interfaces from film and games, one frame per entry: the fastest way to see what reads as an instrument and what reads as decoration. Replaces Territory Studio, whose Blade Runner 2049 page is Vimeo-driven and never finishes loading headless.

screens.title: Teenage Engineering OP-1 field
screens.why: A screen the size of a stamp that shows one thing beautifully; hardware and UI designed as one object, no chrome at all.

screens.title: Nothing
screens.why: Dot-matrix type and monochrome as a whole identity; proof that a product UI can have a typeface as its personality.

screens.title: Vitsœ, Dieter Rams
screens.why: The ten principles and the objects that earned them; the source of 'as little design as possible' that fintech quotes and does not do.

screens.title: Garmin G1000 NXi flight deck
screens.why: A real cockpit display: attitude, tape gauges and a map on one screen, every number sized by how fast it kills you if misread.

screens.title: SpaceX Dragon
screens.why: The crew touchscreens: black, thin white lines, a few large figures; a HUD built by people who could not afford decoration.

screens.title: Flightradar24
screens.why: A live instrument on a map: thousands of moving things and it still reads at a glance, because the map is the layout.

screens.title: Windy
screens.why: Data as a landscape you move through; the wind field is the interface, controls are a thin strip at the edge.

screens.title: Tron: Ares, GMUNK CPU vision (loved on the Atrium run)
screens.why: Rated love for Atrium; on the board so the same eye can say whether it is also right for money.

screens.title: Tron: Ares, GMUNK process (loved on the Atrium run)
screens.why: Rated love for Atrium, has an axis; the densest of the frames he kept.

screens.title: Tron: Ares, GMUNK interface (loved on the Atrium run)
screens.why: Rated love for Atrium; the one that is most nearly a screen someone could use.

screens.title: Tron: Ares, GMUNK LCC0570 (loved on the Atrium run)
screens.why: Rated love for Atrium, has an axis; included as the control for 'dimensions and orbit'.

screens.group: personal data with a point of view
screens.title: Obsidian
screens.why: The graph view Thomas named as the interface he enjoys: your own data as a structure you can see, not a list.

screens.group: personal data with a point of view
screens.title: Claude Code
screens.why: The terminal look he named alongside Obsidian: monospace, one accent, everything visible, nothing hidden behind a hover.

screens.group: personal data with a point of view
screens.title: Warp terminal
screens.why: A terminal rebuilt as a product: blocks, monospace, dense, and still a terminal. The look 'Claude Code' points at, productised.

screens.group: personal data with a point of view
screens.title: WHOOP
screens.why: Personal data with a strong opinion: strain, recovery and sleep as three figures, black ground, no charts you did not ask for.

screens.group: personal data with a point of view
screens.title: Oura
screens.why: The calm end of personal data: three scores, soft type, a single ring. Included as the opposite pole to WHOOP.

screens.group: personal data with a point of view
screens.title: Gyroscope
screens.why: A life as a dashboard, designed to be looked at rather than used: the closest existing thing to 'how should net worth feel'.

screens.group: personal data with a point of view
screens.title: Exist
screens.why: Correlations across everything you track, drawn as plain charts by two people with a point of view; no gamification.

screens.group: personal data with a point of view
screens.title: Strava
screens.why: The one personal-data app people open daily for years; the map and the figures are the design, the chrome is orange and gone.

screens.group: personal data with a point of view
screens.title: Raycast
screens.why: Mac product UI at its most disciplined: one input, dense lists, keyboard first, dark by design rather than by default.

screens.group: personal data with a point of view
screens.title: Things 3
screens.why: The counter-example to density: white, wide, one typeface, and it is still one of the most liked Mac apps ever made.

screens.title: Monzo
screens.why: Control: the UK consumer bank that defined the friendly coral look every fintech then copied.

screens.title: Revolut
screens.why: Control: black, glossy, motion-heavy; the 'premium fintech' template at full strength.

screens.title: Copilot Money
screens.why: Control: the best-reviewed US personal finance app; rounded cards on a gradient, exactly the tells list, done well.

screens.title: Monarch
screens.why: Control: the Mint successor; a net worth chart, a budget, a card per account. The template Numeris currently resembles.

screens.title: Mercury
screens.why: Control: business banking with real typographic taste; the one fintech designers cite. Test of whether taste alone escapes the template.

screens.title: Wise
screens.why: Control: multi-currency, which Numeris is; bright green, big type, and the native-first, converted-second figure done at scale.

screens.title: Emma
screens.why: Control: UK aggregator with a mascot; the far end of 'friendly' and a useful floor.

screens.title: Actual Budget (live demo)
screens.why: Control from the other side: open-source envelope budgeting that looks like a spreadsheet and is loved for it.

screens.title: Firefly III (live demo)
screens.why: Control: the self-hosted finance manager; Bootstrap admin-template finance, so the board has the generic case on it by name.
